questions.q: What are the two contrasting vocal qualities the stage directions assign to Mrs. Pearson and Mrs. Fitzgerald at the opening of the play?
questions.a: Mrs. Pearson speaks in a "light, flurried sort of tone, with a touch of suburban Cockney"; Mrs. Fitzgerald has a "deep voice, rather Irish perhaps." A wrong answer (e.g., both have deep voices) reveals the student missed the explicit stage-direction contrast that foreshadows the personality swap.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Mrs. Pearson refuses Mrs. Fitzgerald's offer to confront the family on her behalf, even though she agrees with the advice.
questions.a: Mrs. Pearson fears "unpleasantness" and lacks the confidence to initiate conflict; she believes the family would resent an outsider's interference and she would be blamed. A wrong answer suggesting she is content with her situation shows failure to infer her internal conflict between desire for respect and fear of confrontation.

questions.q: Apply the "Trait + Evidence + Explanation" formula to prove that Mrs. Pearson (inhabited by Mrs. Fitzgerald) displays assertiveness in her first interaction with Doris.
questions.a: Trait: Assertive. Evidence: She refuses to iron Doris's silk ("Well, this time I don't"), dismisses Doris's complaint about working hard ("I put in twice the hours you do, and get no wages nor thanks"), and criticises Charlie Spence ("Buck teeth and half-witted"). Explanation: Each response rejects automatic compliance, establishes boundaries, and attacks the daughter's sense of entitlement. A weak answer quotes only one line without explaining the pattern.

questions.q: Analyse how the playwright uses the family's speculation about Mrs. Pearson's mental state (concussion, "barmy") to deepen the satire.
questions.a: The family pathologises her assertiveness — Cyril calls her "barmy," Doris suggests concussion — because a mother claiming rights is so alien they assume illness. This satirises the normalized expectation that a mother's default state is self-effacement; any deviation reads as pathology. A superficial answer merely lists the diagnoses without linking to societal expectations.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the play's resolution (Mrs. Pearson reverts to her body but keeps the "firm hand") is a satisfactory feminist ending for a 1950s text.
questions.a: It is a pragmatic, not radical, resolution: she gains respect without permanent personality replacement, suggesting women can claim agency within existing structures. However, it relies on the threat of Mrs. Fitzgerald's return ("keep firm — or you've had it"), implying sustained performance rather than internalised power. A one-sided "yes" or "no" without acknowledging this tension shows incomplete evaluation.

questions.q: Create a 60-word diary entry from Mrs. Pearson's perspective the night after Mrs. Fitzgerald leaves, capturing her internal negotiation between old habits and new resolve.
questions.a: Sample: "They smiled when I suggested rummy. George even said 'whatever you say.' My throat tightened — old Annie would have beamed and rushed to the kitchen. New Annie poured stout, dealt cards, and waited. They'll test me tomorrow. I'll remember the weight of Mrs. Fitzgerald's voice in my throat and not flinch." A weak entry shows only gratitude or only fear, missing the negotiated agency.
